profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a regional French multiple sclerosis (MS) center is being held to align the hospital-based CRC neurology team with the therapeutic education program (TEP) workstream before launching an updated care pathway for patients starting or switching disease-modifying therapy. The context is that the region has recently expanded access to newer MS medications, and the team wants to make referrals, education sessions, and follow-up responsibilities feel seamless across the CRC and the community network. The agenda is to confirm how newly referred patients move from neurology consultation into TEP, what materials and status updates are shared between the two workstreams, how 'high-risk' treatment starts are flagged, and what counts as a completed handoff. The expected outcome is a shared plan for next month's patient cohort, including who sends what information, when education is considered scheduled, and how progress will be reflected in the shared coordination tracker.

members.name: Dr. Claire Moreau
members.expertise: MS diagnosis, disease-modifying therapy selection, risk monitoring pathways, hospital-community coordination
members.background: Claire is a hospital neurologist at the regional MS resource and competence center and has helped implement CRC workflows since the center was approved under the national neurodegenerative diseases plan; she regularly balances specialist treatment decisions with network-wide care coordination.
members.private_state: She wants the CRC to look operationally reliable before an upcoming regional review, so she is trying to reduce loose ends in referrals and ensure that patients starting newer therapies appear fully routed through education and monitoring without creating extra back-and-forth for her clinic.
hidden_assumptions: When a patient is 'entered into TEP,' it means the patient has been accepted into the education pathway and at least the initial education appointment has been booked in the hospital's coordination system.
The 'next month's cohort' refers to patients whose treatment decision has already been finalized in CRC consultation and who are expected to start therapy within the upcoming calendar month.

A 'completed handoff' from neurology to TEP includes transmission of the latest CRC treatment summary, current lab/risk screening results, and the medication-specific vigilance points needed for education.
The shared tracker is the live hospital-network spreadsheet version circulated after last Monday's CRC operations call, which she assumes everyone adopted once the old template was retired.

members.name: Sophie Lambert
members.role: MS nurse educator and TEP program coordinator
members.expertise: Patient therapeutic education, self-management coaching, multidisciplinary session planning, longitudinal patient support
members.background: Sophie is a senior nurse who coordinates the regional MS therapeutic education program across hospital and community settings; she has years of experience adapting education modules to patients' cognitive, social, and psychological needs and often receives referrals from several neurology practices.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the TEP manageable and patient-centered, avoiding situations where patients are booked into formal education before they are emotionally ready or before practical barriers are addressed, while still appearing responsive to the CRC's push for tighter coordination.
hidden_assumptions: When a patient is 'entered into TEP,' it means the referral has been received, triaged, and the patient has been contacted for an educational needs assessment, even if no session is yet booked.
The 'next month's cohort' means all patients newly referred this month who may need education support soon, including those still deciding between therapies or waiting on additional tests.

A 'completed handoff' from neurology mainly means she has enough practical context to make first contact safely; medication-specific risk details can be filled in later during preparation of the education sequence.
The shared tracker is the standing TEP coordination sheet on the network drive that her team updates weekly, and she assumes CRC staff still pull from that file even if they circulate local extracts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say patients should be 'entered into TEP' quickly after consultation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the patient has been formally accepted and the first education session or intake slot is already scheduled in the coordination system.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the referral has been received and the patient has been contacted or queued for an educational assessment, with scheduling to follow later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds administratively routine and both see it as the normal next step after referral, so neither expects that the operational threshold behind the phrase could differ.

misalignment_points.topic: Which patients belong to the 'next month's cohort'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss reviewing 'the cohort for next month' to anticipate education capacity.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means only patients with a confirmed treatment decision and an anticipated start date in the next calendar month.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means all recently referred patients likely to need support soon, including undecided patients and those pending lab clearance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely planning ahead for the same period and use the same planning language, but they silently apply different inclusion criteria because each is anchored in her own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that neurology should make a 'completed handoff' to TEP before therapy start.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the treatment summary, latest MRI/lab status, risk screening, and medication-specific precautions so TEP can educate in a treatment-ready way.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes referral note, patient contact details, and a broad indication of planned therapy, with detailed vigilance content considered outside the initial handoff boundary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They both support smooth transitions and neither wants to sound obstructive, so the phrase 'completed handoff' feels like shared coordination jargon rather than a boundary needing unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to updating 'the spreadsheet' so everyone can see status.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the new CRC operations spreadsheet version circulated after last Monday's call, with columns for treatment decision date and vigilance status.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the longstanding TEP network spreadsheet on the shared drive, organized around referral date, contact attempt, and education modules.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are genuinely shared coordination spreadsheets with overlapping patient names and status fields, so mention of 'the spreadsheet' sounds perfectly unambiguous in conversation even though they are thinking of different files.

turns.inner_thought: We need this pathway to look tight before the regional review. If patients starting the newer therapies next month are all visibly routed through education and monitoring, it will reassure everyone that the CRC is operationally solid. I want fewer loose ends and no chasing people the week before infusion or initiation.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Sophie. With the updated pathway going live, I'd like us to make sure next month runs cleanly from the CRC side into TEP: referrals, timing of the education step, and status visibility, so there aren't gaps between consultation and treatment start.

turns.inner_thought: If we're planning capacity, I need to think broadly: not just the people with a fixed start date, but also the newly referred patients who are hovering around a treatment change, still deciding, or waiting for practical issues to settle. That's what matters for TEP workload and patient-centered pacing.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. From the TEP side we're ready to absorb the flow. It may help if we walk through the cohort for next month, so I can gauge capacity and organize our contact planning early.

turns.inner_thought: For me the cohort for next month is the group already validated in CRC consultation and expected to start within the upcoming calendar month. I want each of those patients entered into TEP immediately after consultation, meaning accepted into the pathway and with the first education or intake slot actually booked in the coordination system.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On our side, I have a handful of patients expected to start next month after CRC review, including a few switches and a couple of new starts, and I'd like each of them entered into TEP right after consultation so the sequence is underway without delay.

turns.inner_thought: That should be manageable if the referrals arrive steadily. Entered into TEP, for me, means we've received the referral, triaged it, and made first contact or at least queued the educational needs assessment. I should also keep room for patients still finalizing a decision, because they often need support before anything formal is booked.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can do that. Once the referrals come through, I can have those patients entered into TEP within a few days, and I would also include some of the people who are still settling their decision if they look like they'll need support early.

turns.inner_thought: I need the handoff to be truly complete before therapy start: CRC treatment summary, latest lab and risk screening status, and the vigilance points specific to the medication so education is treatment-ready. I don't want any appearance that education happened without the right safety frame.
turns.utterance: Good. One point I'd like to lock down is that before any therapy start, there should be a completed handoff to TEP, with enough behind it that the education step doesn't miss treatment-specific vigilance issues.

turns.inner_thought: That's reasonable. For us, a completed handoff is usually enough information to start safely: the referral note, contact details, and a broad sense of the planned therapy. The finer vigilance details can be picked up afterward when we shape the sequence. I don't want the first contact blocked by waiting for every technical element.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's fine. In practice, once I have the referral note, the planned treatment, and the patient's contact details, the handoff is usually complete enough for my team to begin outreach and prepare the next steps.

turns.inner_thought: We need one live view, and I mean the new CRC operations spreadsheet from Monday's call, not the old local versions. I want to be able to open it and verify who is actually booked, who is cleared from the monitoring side, and who still needs action. That visibility matters for the review and for my clinic flow.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Then let's keep everything visible in the spreadsheet so the CRC team can quickly see who is booked, who is cleared, and who still needs follow-up as start dates come closer.

turns.inner_thought: That's already what we're doing on the TEP coordination sheet on the network drive. My team updates it every Friday with referral status, contact attempts, and progression through the modules. As long as they keep checking that file, they should have what they need.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's easy on our side. The team already updates the spreadsheet every Friday with referral status, patient contact attempts, and how people are moving through the modules, so we can keep that current.

turns.inner_thought: Especially for the higher-risk treatments, I need early visibility on the patients who are definitely starting next month, and I need to know the handoff is fully complete and education is actually booked, not just pending. Those are the cases that could reflect badly if anything slips between consult and start.
turns.utterance: And for the higher-risk starts, I'd really like the cohort for next month to be visible as early as possible so nothing falls between the CRC consultation, the completed handoff, and education booking.

turns.inner_thought: Early visibility helps us because I can reach people before the formal sequence is fixed, even if they are still wavering or waiting on tests. That makes the process gentler and usually avoids bottlenecks later. I don't need a fixed schedule yet to start supporting them.
turns.utterance: I agree. Early visibility helps us as well, because we can contact patients before the formal sequence is fixed, which usually reduces delays once the plan starts moving.

turns.inner_thought: So neurology will send the post-consultation cases, and I expect to see them entered into TEP in the sense of accepted with an initial slot booked, and marked in the new CRC spreadsheet before their treatment dates get too close. If I can verify that easily, this process will feel under control.
turns.utterance: All right. So neurology will send over the next set after consultation, and then I'll look for them as entered into TEP and marked in the spreadsheet well before the start dates approach.

turns.inner_thought: That works. We'll receive the referrals, treat the handoff as complete enough to start outreach once the core context is there, and keep our TEP sheet updated through the month. As long as we're responsive and patients are contacted quickly, the pathway should feel smooth without overcommitting them too early.
turns.utterance: Very good. We'll take the referrals, complete the handoff on our side, and keep the spreadsheet current for the upcoming month so everyone can follow progress.
